sections.html:
Alton is a Mississippi River city in Madison County, about 18 miles north of St. Louis, with a low-priced housing market. Owners value their homes at a typical $103,700, and 59.9% of homes are owner-occupied, so a good part of the market is rental. Gross rent runs a typical $1,015.

The city had 25,676 residents in 2020 and an estimated 25,013 on July 1, 2025, a 2.6% drop. Most of Alton rises steeply from the waterfront onto bluffs, which gives many streets river views and leaves low-lying blocks exposed to river floods. Older housing is often Victorian Queen Anne, with brick-paved streets left over from the area's brick factories.

These affect inspections, insurance and buyer expectations more than any other local factor. The lower levels of Alton flood, high-water marks are painted on the grain silos near the riverfront, and the flood of 1993 was the worst of the last century. The city has held an open house on planned flood mitigation, so ask City Hall about any project near your block.

Buyers near the river will ask about the flood zone. Gather any elevation certificate, flood insurance history and repair invoices before you list, and answer questions about past water plainly. Buyers of Victorian-era houses tend to ask about wiring, roofs and foundations, so have dates for any updates ready.

The planning department administers the Riverfront TIF District and the Hunterstown TIF District and works with Madison County on the Riverbend Enterprise Zone. A property inside one of those boundaries may qualify for redevelopment incentives, which can matter to a buyer planning to renovate. Ask the Planning and Development office at 618.463.3500 whether your parcel is inside one.

Alton's Code Enforcement Department performs universal residential occupancy inspections, so a change of occupant can trigger a visit even when ownership stays the same. The department also issues building, demolition, electrical, plumbing, signage, occupancy and agent authorization permits and reviews plans for renovations.

  • Since February 1, 2015, the city has refused to schedule an occupancy inspection until the form names every person moving into the dwelling.
  • For adults the form needs a full name, date of birth and driver's license or state ID number. For children it needs a full name and date of birth.
  • The department cites weeds, junk, trash, derelict vehicles and exterior or interior maintenance violations, and it sends unresolved citations to court.
  • The city also inspects fire-damaged structures and handles demolition proceedings.

Before you list, call the Code Enforcement Office at 618.463.3500 and ask whether the property has open citations or an unclosed permit. A buyer takes on those issues along with the house, so settling them first keeps the closing date steady.

Madison County collects in four installments. Bills for the 2025 tax year went out the week of June 9, 2026, and mobile home tax came due August 31.

2026 installment dates from the Madison County Treasurer
InstallmentDue date in 2026
FirstJuly 9
SecondSeptember 9
ThirdOctober 9
FourthDecember 9

Call the Treasurer's Office at (618) 692-6260 for a duplicate bill. State law makes the tax due even when the bill never arrives.

• A 1.5% penalty attaches to a late installment every 30 days, and taxes still unpaid go into the annual tax sale.
  • After a tax sale an owner can redeem for two to three years through the County Clerk, paying the entire amount owed.
  • About 220 taxing districts levy against Madison County property, and the assessed value is one third of fair market value.
  • Exemptions include a $6,000 general homestead, a $5,000 senior homestead, $5,000 for returning service members and $2,000 for persons with disabilities.
  • Madison County does not apply the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law that caps increases in other counties.

Before closing, get a payoff figure from the Treasurer so the title company can pay any open installment from the seller's proceeds.

A written complaint goes to the Madison County Board of Review, and it is due 30 days after the assessments are published. Section 16-55(d) of the Property Tax Code sets that deadline. Talk first with the township or county assessor, since the Chief County Assessment Office at (618) 692-6270 can explain how the value was set.

You will need evidence that the property is overassessed, such as recent sales of similar Alton houses, an appraisal or documented condition problems. The Board of Review can be reached at (618) 692-6210. An appeal changes the assessed value only, because the tax rate comes from the local taxing districts.

sections.h2: What the Madison County Recorder needs for a deed
sections.html:
The Recorder will not accept a deed without an Illinois Department of Revenue transfer declaration (PTAX) or a statement of exemption. The state collects 50 cents on each $500 of taxable consideration under Section 31-10 of the Property Tax Code, and Madison County adds 25 cents on each $500.

  • Each deed carries the grantee's name and address for tax billing, with a Plat Act affidavit attached.
  • A permanent parcel number is required on documents that affect a transfer, by county board resolution.
  • The preparer's name and address must appear on the instrument itself.
  • When paying by check, the recording fee and the transfer tax are paid separately.

Executor's, administrator's, guardian's and trustee's deeds are recorded here too, so a house sold through an estate follows the same declaration and parcel number rules.

sections.h2: Which selling route fits an Alton house?
sections.html:
Alton owners can hire an agent, sell privately, or sell outright to a buyer who takes whatever shape the house is in. A listing works best on a clean, move-in ready house. A private sale suits an owner who already has a buyer lined up. The third route suits a vacant, inherited or damaged house, because the buyer accepts what is there and the closing date can be set around the occupancy inspection and any flood or code questions.

Start by calling Code Enforcement, then the Treasurer for a balance, and put the results in one folder for the buyer or title company.

sections.h2: A simple order of steps for an Alton seller
sections.html: Sellers who work in a fixed order tend to avoid last-minute surprises. First, call Code Enforcement and ask about open citations, unclosed permits and whether an occupancy inspection will be needed for the next occupant. Second, ask the Treasurer which installments are paid and what the payoff is. Third, pick a route and a title company. Fourth, make sure the title company has the parcel number, because Madison County requires it on transfer documents. Last, confirm who signs the transfer declaration and who pays the recording fee and transfer tax at closing.

faqs.q: How many property tax installments does Madison County have?
faqs.a: Four. For 2025 taxes payable in 2026 they were due July 9, September 9, October 9 and December 9, with mobile home tax due August 31. The Treasurer's Office can give you the schedule on the next bill.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for a late Madison County installment?
faqs.a: A 1.5% penalty is added the day after the deadline and again every 30 days. Delinquency notices go out about a month before the tax sale, and unpaid taxes are sold to a tax buyer.

faqs.q: Does Alton require an occupancy inspection when I sell?
faqs.a: Alton conducts universal residential occupancy inspections and needs information on every person who will live in the dwelling. Ask Code Enforcement at 618.463.3500 whether your sale or the next tenant triggers one.

faqs.q: How much is the Illinois transfer tax on an Alton sale?
faqs.a: The state rate is 50 cents on each $500 of declared value, and Madison County adds 25 cents on each $500. The Recorder collects both at recording.

faqs.q: When must an Alton assessment complaint be filed?
faqs.a: Within 30 days of publication of the assessments, and the complaint goes to the Madison County Board of Review. Call (618) 692-6210 to learn how the board takes filings.
